hypotheses.observation: The same immutable input tensor feeds an elementwise path and a row-wise reduction at separated graph points.
hypotheses.mechanism: Preserving each thread's loaded input values across the reduction can eliminate a second global-memory read.
hypotheses.transformation: Load each thread's row elements once, retain them in registers, perform the row reduction, then consume the retained values for the elementwise path.
preconditions: Register capacity is sufficient for the retained values.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially lower global-memory traffic and improved performance from increased input reuse.
risks: Register allocation may increase occupancy loss or spills.
The reduction and elementwise scheduling may increase synchronization or instruction overhead.
unknowns: The current amount of global traffic is unknown.
Whether compiler allocation causes spills is unknown.
required_evidence: Register allocation and spill statistics for the transformed kernel.
Global load transactions or bytes for both paths.
Occupancy and runtime comparison against the baseline.

hypotheses.observation: One logical row is assigned to one thread block, and the input is immutable between separated uses.
hypotheses.mechanism: Block-level staging in shared memory can provide a reusable copy when retaining the whole row in registers is too costly.
hypotheses.transformation: Cooperatively load the row into shared memory, synchronize around the reduction, and reuse the staged values for the elementwise path.
preconditions: The row fits within available shared memory.
Synchronization is valid for all block participants.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially reduce repeated global loads while limiting per-thread register growth.
risks: Synchronization and bank conflicts may offset reuse benefits.
The row may exceed shared-memory capacity.
unknowns: Row size and shared-memory footprint are unknown.
The baseline and transformed global traffic are unknown.
required_evidence: Global-memory transaction counts and runtime comparison.

hypotheses.observation: The two separated use sites are connected by a row-wise reduction, while each row is confined to one block.
hypotheses.mechanism: Fusing the reduction and elementwise work into one block-level execution can avoid materializing or rereading intermediate row data across separate kernels or graph stages.
hypotheses.transformation: Combine the row reduction and elementwise computation in one block, retaining reusable values in registers or shared memory as needed.
preconditions: The operation order permits fusion without changing required semantics.
The complete row and reduction fit the block's resource limits.
Any required block synchronization is supported.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially reduce kernel-launch and intermediate-memory overhead and improve locality.
risks: Fusion may increase register or shared-memory pressure.
Longer kernels may reduce occupancy or expose synchronization costs.
The elementwise operation may not be schedulable after the reduction without additional barriers.
unknowns: Whether the separated points are separate kernels is unknown.
Intermediate materialization and launch overhead are unknown.
Register pressure and global traffic are unknown.
required_evidence: Register, shared-memory, occupancy, and spill measurements.
Global-memory traffic and end-to-end runtime comparison.
